intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the exercises with a pencil, answer the recall questions without looking, and write your own notes in the margins beside mine.

sections.title: What the Software Does, and Does Not
sections.big_idea: QDA software is **a filing system for evidence**. It stores, retrieves and counts. The meaning, the themes and the claims stay with you.
in_plain_words: Before software, forty interviews were coded with highlighters and index cards, and that still works. What changes is speed and tidiness: retrieval is instant, the codebook stays consistent, the audit trail builds itself and a team's work can be merged.

Five tools are worth knowing: Taguette and QualCoder are free, and NVivo, MAXQDA and ATLAS.ti are commercial. They differ in interface more than in what they let you conclude. **Decide your method first**, because software cannot tell which method you are following.

key_terms.meaning: Qualitative data analysis software; the program does the bookkeeping only.
A label you attach to a segment of data.
A fact about a participant, such as district or age band.
A dated note recording your thinking.
An exchange format that moves a project between tools.

worked_example.title: Is software worth it here?
worked_example.setup: Three studies, judged by the slide's rule of thumb: roughly a dozen sources or two coders.
steps: Study 1 has six interviews and one analyst, so it falls below the threshold and a Word matrix will do.
Study 2 has forty interviews in two languages and two coders, so it is well above it.
Study 3 has 200 open-ended survey answers and wants counts, so a simple tool such as Taguette fits.
Study 4 has audio focus groups needing who-said-what coding, so choose a fuller tool.
worked_example.answer: Study 1 marginal, Study 2 yes, Study 3 a simple tool, Study 4 a fuller tool.

mistakes: Treating the software as the analysis. A project of 240 codes and no argument has a filing system and nothing else.
Opening the program before stating the method, which leaves inductive thematic analysis by default.
Using word clouds as findings. The slides call them of little use.

recall.q: What does QDA software do and not do?
recall.a: It does the bookkeeping of analysis. It does not do the analysis.

recall.q: Which two of the five tools in the deck are free?
recall.a: Taguette and QualCoder.

recall.q: What is the rough threshold for software to pay off?
recall.a: About a dozen sources or two coders.

recall.q: Why can a team choose any tool?
recall.a: Every tool can export a project in the REFI-QDA exchange format.

sections.title: Preparing the Data
sections.big_idea: Coding is only as good as the data under it. **Consent, transcription, translation and attributes** come first and take a week for 36 interviews.
in_plain_words: Three consent answers decide your workflow: recording and transcription, quotation, and processing by an outside service. A 'no' to the last removes most cloud and AI features. Transcribe in the language spoken, check machine output against the audio, and choose a translation workflow on purpose.

Name files by a convention, keep one file per interview, and import attributes from a spreadsheet. Leave the respondent's grammar and the interviewer's questions alone. **Cleaning speech into prose is editing the data.**

diagram.caption: the order of preparation before the first code

key_terms.meaning: Every word, with fillers and false starts removed.
Replace names with IDs and keep the key apart.
Code the source language, translate everything, or run both side by side.
One row per file, one column per fact.
A native speaker reads the transcript against the audio.

worked_example.title: Plan the transcription hours
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 10 hours of audio transcribed by hand. The deck gives 4 to 6 hours per audio hour for intelligent verbatim and 6 to 8 for full verbatim.
steps: Intelligent verbatim, low end: 10 × 4 = 40 hours.
Intelligent verbatim, high end: 10 × 6 = 60 hours.
Full verbatim, low end: 10 × 6 = 60 hours.
Full verbatim, high end: 10 × 8 = 80 hours.
Name the file for interview 14 in Bihar in Hindi using the convention: INT_BR_014_HI.
worked_example.answer: 40 to 60 hours for intelligent verbatim, 60 to 80 for full verbatim.

mistakes: Translating everything into English and coding the translation without saying so. It is the commonest workflow and the one that loses most.
Importing machine transcripts without a native-speaker check against the audio.
Editing text inside the QDA project after coding has started, which can detach codes from passages.

recall.q: Which three consent questions shape the workflow?
recall.a: Recording and transcription, quotation, and processing by an external service.

recall.q: What does workflow C do?
recall.a: It keeps the source and the translation side by side, coding on the source.

recall.q: Why include the interviewer as an attribute?
recall.a: Interviewer effects are real and a matrix by interviewer is a quality check.

recall.q: What is the file name convention in the deck?
recall.a: TYPE_SITE_ID_LANG, for example INT_WB_022_BN.

recall.q: Where should cleaning be done?
recall.a: In a word processor before import.

sections.title: The Coding Workflow
sections.big_idea: A code is **a label with a definition**, and the codebook gets its quality at the revision after five transcripts.
in_plain_words: First-cycle coding labels the data. Second-cycle coding groups the labels into categories and themes. Read every transcript once, start from defined a priori codes, code five transcripts closely, revise the codebook, and recode those five before you code the rest.

Keep the hierarchy to two or three levels, with about 40 to 80 codes after revision for a focused 36-interview study. Write memos at every decision and surprise. A theme is a claim you build, so **the code tree is not your findings**.

diagram.caption: the seven-step cycle, with write-up to follow

key_terms.meaning: Name, definition, use, do-not-use rule, example and source for each code.
A code named with the respondent's own phrase.
The passage a code attaches to; a sentence or two is typical.
Further data add no new codes or refine no themes.
A claim built across codes and cases.

worked_example.title: Budget the coding time
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 240 transcript pages to code. The deck says a person reading with a defined codebook manages about 8 to 12 pages an hour.
steps: At the fast end: 240 ÷ 12 = 20 hours.
At the slow end: 240 ÷ 8 = 30 hours.
Add the revision and recoding of the first five transcripts to the plan.
Write the memo for each decision as you go.
worked_example.answer: 20 to 30 hours of coding, before revision and recoding.

mistakes: Writing a code name with no definition. A code without one is a guess about what you meant, made later by you.
Skipping the recode of the first five transcripts after the codebook changes.
Claiming saturation with no code-creation curve to show it.
Reporting auto-coding by text search as coding. It finds words and misses meanings.

recall.q: What does a full codebook entry contain?
recall.a: Name, definition, use when, do not use when, example and source.

recall.q: Why recode the first five transcripts?
recall.a: They were coded with a codebook that no longer exists.

recall.q: How many codes should a focused 36-interview study end with?
recall.a: Perhaps 40 to 80 after revision.

recall.q: What can the software show about saturation?
recall.a: When new codes stopped appearing, as a count of codes created per transcript.

recall.q: What is the difference between a code and a theme?
recall.a: A code labels data; a theme is a claim built across codes and cases.

sections.title: Taguette: The Free Start
sections.big_idea: Taguette is a **ten-minute start** for text coding. When you build the same pivot table by hand a third time, move on.
in_plain_words: Taguette runs in a browser, either locally or on a server, and handles text only. You highlight a passage, give it tags, and export everything. Definitions live in the tag description, hierarchy comes from punctuation such as SAVINGS.shield, and merging tags turns first-cycle codes into second-cycle ones.

Its best export is the all-highlights CSV. Joined with an attribute sheet, it supports every count in section 07 through pivot tables. A self-hosted server gives small teams collaboration while **data stays inside the institution**.

left.title: Taguette does
items: Show every highlight for a tag
Export to Word, CSV and HTML
Let a team tag on a server

right.title: Move to a fuller tool for

key_terms.meaning: Taguette's word for a code.
A selected passage carrying one or more tags.
SAVINGS.shield style naming that builds a hierarchy.
Document, tag and text, ready for counting in a spreadsheet.
The whole project, kept as a backup.

worked_example.title: Read the mini-study table
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: the Bihar mini-study of 12 interviews. SAVINGS.shield has 14 highlights in 8 documents.
steps: Documents with the tag: 8 of 12.
Documents without it: 12 − 8 = 4.
Read the 14 highlights as a group, since this export is the evidence for the theme memo.
Ask which of the four others share a feature, which needs an attribute query done in the spreadsheet.
worked_example.answer: The tag appears in 8 documents and is absent from 4; the 4 are the next thing to read.

mistakes: Using the hosted version for transcripts the consent form does not allow on an outside server.
Trying to code audio in Taguette, which takes text only.
Keeping analytic memos in tag descriptions, which are meant for definitions.

recall.q: Which file types does Taguette accept?
recall.a: Text formats such as .docx, .pdf, .txt, .html, .odt, .rtf and .epub; no audio or video.

recall.q: How do you build a hierarchy in Taguette?
recall.a: With punctuation in the tag name, for example SAVINGS.shield.

recall.q: Why is the all-highlights CSV useful?
recall.a: It supports counts and pivot tables by attribute when joined with an attribute sheet.

recall.q: How do two coders check agreement in Taguette?
recall.a: They tag the same documents with distinct prefixed tag sets, export and compare in a spreadsheet.

sections.title: QualCoder: Free and Full
sections.big_idea: QualCoder offers **most of a commercial tool for nothing**, offline, on a modest laptop.
in_plain_words: QualCoder codes text, PDF, images, audio and video. It has a code tree with categories, memos, cases and attributes, coding reports, a co-occurrence matrix and a coder comparison with kappa. Projects exchange through REFI-QDA, so you are never locked in.

Day to day, the coding workspace does the work, the reports do the analysis and the journals hold the thinking. Set the coder name before the first code. **Audio coding is the feature that justifies leaving Taguette**, with timestamps every minute making transcript and recording scroll together.

key_terms.meaning: A participant, who may appear across several files.
The setting the comparison report depends on.
A note on a passage with no code, for 'come back to this'.
Segments for chosen codes, filtered by file, case or attribute.
The REFI-QDA project file.

worked_example.title: Count the files in the SHG project
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 36 source-language transcripts and 36 English translations, imported as one project, with 12 audio files linked to transcripts.
steps: Files imported: 36 + 36 = 72.
Cases: one per participant, so 36.
Audio is linked to transcripts, so it adds no cases.
Two coders each code their own language, plus four of the other's translations.

mistakes: Forgetting to set the coder name before coding, which breaks the comparison report.
Searching Indic text for a word and expecting inflections to match. There is no stemming.
Turning on the optional AI features without thinking through where the data go.

recall.q: What does QualCoder need to code audio and video?
recall.a: VLC installed.

recall.q: Which report compares two coders?
recall.a: The coder comparison, giving percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa.

recall.q: What is the REFI-QDA standard for?
recall.a: Moving a project between tools without losing the coding.

recall.q: How do you use annotations versus memos in QualCoder?
recall.a: Annotations for 'come back to this', memos for 'this is why'.

sections.title: NVivo, MAXQDA and ATLAS.ti
sections.big_idea: The three commercial tools do the same job with **three different organising ideas**. Pick the one your team can open.
in_plain_words: NVivo is built around files, codes and cases with a query menu as its analytic engine. MAXQDA shows four windows at once, and its activation move makes retrieval visible. ATLAS.ti treats each selected passage as a quotation object that you can link to others.

Check licences, trials and data terms before you pay, and ask vendors in writing where your data is stored. Choose by what your institution licenses, what platform your team uses and what the study needs. **None of them makes a weak analysis strong.**

diagram.caption: strengths as the deck describes them

key_terms.meaning: NVivo's codes-by-attributes table.
MAXQDA's way of choosing documents and codes for retrieval.
ATLAS.ti's passage object with its own ID.
MAXQDA's summary per document per code.
NVivo's cases-by-themes table with typed summaries.

worked_example.title: Match tool to situation
worked_example.setup: Use the decision table to choose for four teams.
steps: A team on Mac with a mixed-methods survey: MAXQDA, which has feature parity across platforms and a Stats module.
A policy client wants framework analysis: NVivo or MAXQDA, for the built-in charting step.
A discourse study linking passages: ATLAS.ti, for quotations and networks.
A team with no budget: QualCoder or Taguette.
worked_example.answer: MAXQDA, NVivo or MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti, QualCoder or Taguette.

mistakes: Buying before checking what the library already licenses.
Uploading transcripts to a cloud version before reading the vendor's data terms.
Using NVivo's sentiment coding or word-frequency options on Indian-language text as evidence.

recall.q: Which tool has the gentlest learning curve?
recall.a: MAXQDA.

recall.q: What is the 'quotation' in ATLAS.ti?
recall.a: A selected passage that becomes an object with its own ID, whether or not it is coded.

recall.q: What four things should you ask a vendor in writing?
recall.a: Where data is stored, who can access it, whether it trains models, and how to delete it.

recall.q: What does the general advice say about choosing?
recall.a: Use the tool closest to hand for a first project, the team's agreed tool for a team, and learn two for a career.

sections.title: Queries, Matrices and Visuals
sections.big_idea: Retrieval is the analysis. **Read the passages first**, then let matrices tell you which passage set to read next.
in_plain_words: A retrieval gathers every segment for a code across all the interviews. Filtering it by attribute gives you a comparison. Matrices cross codes with attributes, and co-occurrence tables show which ideas appear together. Each is a pointer into the text, never a result by itself.

Charting cases by themes in a framework matrix is the analysis itself. When you write a claim, trace it back through memo, query, retrieval and segments. **A matrix cell is never a population proportion**, because the sample was purposive.

diagram.caption: the chain of evidence from query to claim

key_terms.meaning: All segments for a code, read together.
Segments where two codes overlap.
Cases by themes, each cell a short summary.
A search for codes within a set distance.
A case that contradicts a theme.

worked_example.title: Plan the framework matrix
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 36 cases charted against 8 themes, which the deck says takes about three days.
steps: Cells to fill: 36 × 8 = 288.
Per day over three days: 288 ÷ 3 = 96 cells.
Each cell is a short summary with a phrase quoted, written from the retrievals.
Read down a column for the range of a theme, across a row for one woman's account.
worked_example.answer: 288 cells, about 96 a day for three days.

mistakes: Reporting a matrix cell as a share of a population when the sample was chosen on purpose.
Reading segment counts as importance. They mostly show how much people talked.
Drawing a hairball network or a word cloud and calling it analysis.
Counting before you have read the whole retrieval.

recall.q: Why report files before segments in a matrix?
recall.a: Segment counts reflect talkativeness and segment size; files show how many people raised it.

recall.q: What does a co-occurrence table do?
recall.a: It finds where to look; you still read the overlapping segments.

recall.q: What is the best qualitative figure in most reports?
recall.a: A table of quotations by theme and case, or a framework matrix.

recall.q: What do word-frequency queries return on a Hindi corpus?
recall.a: Postpositions such as hai, ka, ki, ko and mein.

sections.title: Coding in Teams
sections.big_idea: A team needs **one codebook, one owner and an early test merge**. Measure agreement per code, act on it, then measure again.
in_plain_words: Teams give capacity, languages and a second reading. Each coder sets a name in the software, the codebook owner decides all new codes, and coders propose changes in a memo. Weekly meetings put the segments on screen and log decisions.

Cohen's kappa corrects percentage agreement for chance. Report it for each code separately, and use it only when the method expects consistent coding. **A low kappa is a finding about the definition**, so the fix is in the codebook and then a recode of the shared sample.

key_terms.meaning: Agreement between two coders, corrected for chance.
How segment boundaries are drawn; it drives the agreement number.
The person who adds codes to the master and versions it.
Each coder works on a copy; a master imports each.
A dated memo of decisions.

worked_example.title: Read an agreement table
worked_example.setup: Illustrative round 1 kappas: SAVINGS_PURPOSE 0.84, SAVINGS_BARRIER 0.76, SAVINGS_SHIELD 0.58, DECISION_STRATEGY 0.52. The deck calls above 0.8 strong and 0.6 to 0.8 moderate to substantial.
steps: PURPOSE at 0.84 is strong; no action.
BARRIER at 0.76 is moderate to substantial; no action.
SHIELD at 0.58 and STRATEGY at 0.52 fall under 0.6, so both need work.
SHIELD was redefined and reached 0.79 in round 2: 0.79 − 0.58 = 0.21 gain.
STRATEGY was split into three codes, then re-measured.
worked_example.answer: Two codes needed work; SHIELD gained 0.21 after redefinition.

mistakes: Merging for the first time on the deadline. Test with two small copies in week two.
Reporting one kappa for forty codes.
Measuring agreement once at the start and never again.
Applying kappa to reflexive thematic analysis, where agreement is not the goal.

recall.q: Who may create codes in the divide-and-merge arrangement?
recall.a: Only the codebook owner; coders propose in a memo.

recall.q: What share of files is a standard shared sample?
recall.a: 10 to 20 per cent.

recall.q: Why is percentage agreement high even when coding is poor?
recall.a: Most text is uncoded and both coders agree it is; kappa corrects for that.

recall.q: What does agreement on English translations test across languages?
recall.a: Whether the codebook travels; it does not show whether the coders read the languages alike.

sections.title: Mixed Methods
sections.big_idea: Surveys and interviews should **answer each other**. Attributes from the survey make every qualitative matrix a mixed-methods table.
in_plain_words: Integration can happen at the design, in the methods (connecting, building, merging) or at interpretation through joint displays. Interviewees sampled from the survey carry their survey values as attributes, which lets you pick them on purpose, for example high gainers, no change and decliners.

Open-ended survey answers count as qualitative data at scale, and counts are legitimate there because the denominator is the survey sample. For a purposive set of interviews, a count only locates evidence. **The rule is the denominator.**

children.label: At the design
items: One strand informs the other's design

key_terms.meaning: Interviewees are sampled from the survey.
Interview findings become items in the next survey.
Both sets of results interpreted in one table.
Survey result, qualitative finding and integrated reading side by side.
Turning coded text into counts or variables.

worked_example.title: Which count is legitimate?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 480 survey respondents answered an open question and 31% cited distance.
steps: The sample is the survey's and every respondent answered, so the denominator is known.
People citing distance: 480 × 0.31 = 149.
This is a proportion, reported with the n and the multiple-response note.
'42% of women in the district feel the group protects savings' from 36 purposive interviews fails, because the sample cannot support a population figure.
worked_example.answer: About 149 of 480 is a statistic; the 42% claim from 36 interviews is not.

mistakes: Reporting survey and interview chapters that never touch.
Presenting a purposive count as a population proportion.
Hiding a disagreement between strands. The slide shows it can explain a survey null.
Linking interviewees to survey records without consent for the join.

recall.q: What does the third column of a joint display hold?
recall.a: The integrated reading of the survey and qualitative findings.

recall.q: Which tool was built with mixed methods in mind?
recall.a: MAXQDA.

recall.q: Why are deviant cases valuable?
recall.a: They are selected on purpose and are often the most informative interviews.

recall.q: How do coded open-ends rejoin the survey data?
recall.a: As a case-by-code 0/1 matrix joined by ID.

recall.q: What is the one rule for deciding whether a count is evidence?
recall.a: Check the denominator.

sections.title: Rigour and Reporting
sections.big_idea: The project file **is** the audit trail. Keep it as you go and rigour becomes routine.
in_plain_words: Lincoln and Guba's four criteria are credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Each has a practice and a trace in the project: retrievals and negative cases, attributes and sampling memos, the log and codebook versions, reflexive memos and a second reader.

Report with COREQ or SRQR, show quotations with their range and consent status, and keep a quotation log. Deposit what consent allows, usually the codebook and coded project without transcripts. **A methods paragraph is believed when every clause points to a file.**

key_terms.meaning: The records letting a reader follow every step.
The researcher's position written down for the reader.
Taking findings back to participants.
Reporting checklists with 32 and 21 items.
One row per quotation: source, language, consent.

worked_example.title: Answer the examiner
worked_example.setup: An examiner asks: 'Show me how you got from the interviews to theme three.'
steps: Open the memo dated before the theme was named.
Show the matrix cell that pointed you to the pattern.
Show the retrieval behind it.
Show three cases, including one that did not fit.
worked_example.answer: A dated memo, a matrix, a retrieval and three cases including a negative one.

mistakes: Treating member checking of transcripts as strong evidence. Checking synthesised findings is higher value and harder.
Leaving out a reflexivity sentence where a finding could reflect the researcher's position.
Quoting with identifying detail in a small village.
Depositing audio, which rarely has consent.

recall.q: What does dependability ask?
recall.a: Whether the process was consistent and could be followed.

recall.q: What belongs in a quotation log?
recall.a: Report page, pseudonym, source file, segment, language and consent status.

recall.q: Which objects can you always deposit?
recall.a: The codebook with versions, the blank interview guide and consent forms, and the sampling memo.

recall.q: When should the first reflexive memo be written?
recall.a: Before the first interview.

sections.title: AI, Choosing a Tool, and Practice
sections.big_idea: Every AI feature sends transcripts to an outside model. **Validate it like a second coder, or do not use it**, and disclose either way.
in_plain_words: ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA and NVivo offer opt-in AI features, QualCoder offers optional ones using your own key, and Taguette has none. The first fact about each is that transcript text leaves your machine, which depends on your consent and policy. Risks include hallucinated summaries, homogenised codes and weak Indian-language performance.

If you code with a model, give it the codebook, have it code the files a human coded and report kappa per code. Use it only where it agrees. Then choose a tool, plan the work and write the disclosure. **Invest in the codebook, memos and archive**, since the software is where they live this year.

diagram.caption: validating AI coding as a second coder

key_terms.meaning: A summary stating something no participant said.
Codes drift into one style and lose local nuance.
Agreement between a person and the model on a code.
Tool, version, data seen, consent basis and the limit of its role.
A model run on your own machine so data stay put.

worked_example.title: Compare human-model with human-human
worked_example.setup: Illustrative table: SAVINGS_PURPOSE 0.84 human-human and 0.77 human-model; SAVINGS_SHIELD 0.79 and 0.41.
steps: PURPOSE gap: 0.84 − 0.77 = 0.07, a small gap.
SHIELD gap: 0.79 − 0.41 = 0.38, a large one.
PURPOSE is descriptive, so use the model for a first pass that a human reviews.
SHIELD is interpretive and became a study finding, so it stays human only.
worked_example.answer: Model first pass for PURPOSE; human only for SHIELD.

mistakes: Uploading transcripts to an AI feature without consent that names external processing.
Accepting an AI summary or code without checking it against the retrieval.
Reporting AI-coded Hindi transcripts as human thematic analysis.
Costing the review as a tenth of the coding time. It takes about half.

recall.q: Which tool in the deck has no AI feature?
recall.a: Taguette.

recall.q: What are the five risks the deck lists?
recall.a: Data leaving the machine, hallucinated summaries, homogenisation, weak Indian-language performance and undisclosed use.

recall.q: What question will a referee ask about AI coding?
recall.a: What did the model code that a human would not have, and what did it miss?

recall.q: What is the last row's general principle in the choosing table?
recall.a: The tool may change; the codebook and the archive should not.

recall.q: When should you write the AI disclosure?
recall.a: Before the analysis.

notes.2: Use this agenda as your **map for the whole course**. Sections 02, 03 and 07 to 10 describe the work and apply in any tool. Sections 04 to 06 describe the tools. If you already own a licence, read the work sections first and the tool section for your program second.
notes.4: Hold on to the last sentence of the definition: the software does the bookkeeping and **you do the analysis**. A project with 240 codes and no argument is what happens when the filing gets easy and the thinking waits. Ask of every feature whether it stores, retrieves or displays.
notes.5: Read this as a menu sorted by price. Two free tools, Taguette and QualCoder, cover the coding workflow in full. The three paid tools differ in interface more than in what you can conclude. Note the last line: **every tool exports to REFI-QDA**, so your first choice is not a trap.
notes.6: Write the method into your protocol before you open any program. Without a stated method, unstructured coding turns into inductive thematic analysis **by default**. Notice that content analysis alone treats the software's counts as the result. In the other five methods the counts only point you to passages.
notes.7: Use this table to decide whether to install anything. The rule of thumb at the bottom is **about a dozen sources or two coders**. Below that line a framework matrix in Word can do the job. Above it, hand methods leave you with a filing system nobody can search.
notes.8: Treat this table as a translation dictionary. A highlight in Taguette is a reference in NVivo and a quotation in ATLAS.ti. The course uses plain words (source, segment, code, attribute, memo, matrix). Once you know the ideas, **a new package takes about a week to learn**.
notes.9: Run through the five differences and mark the ones that apply to your study. The costliest is the habit of translating everything into English first. **Test word counts and auto-coding on your own language** before you trust them, because inflected languages behave unpredictably.
notes.10: The eight steps run from preparation to decision. Sections 02, 03 and 07 to 10 are about the work, so they apply whatever the tool. One illustrative study runs through all of them: 36 interviews in Hindi and Bangla about savings. **Follow its numbers from slide to slide.**
notes.12: Settle consent before you import a single recording. Three answers decide the workflow: recording and transcription, quotation, and **processing by an outside service**. A 'no' to the last removes most cloud and AI features. Record each answer as an attribute so the software can filter on it.
notes.13: Choose the transcription level to match the question. Intelligent verbatim suits most applied work; full verbatim suits discourse analysis. Machine output saves hours but still needs **a human who heard the interview**. Transcribe in the spoken language and script, and keep translation as a separate decision.
notes.14: Pick A, B or C on purpose and write it down. Workflow A loses least and needs coders in each language. Workflow B is the commonest and loses idiom, tone and the respondent's own word. **Keep source-language terms** for concepts such as sharam and lajja, and say in the report which route you took.
notes.15: Use this table as an import checklist. Give each interview its own file and a header with its attributes. Check that scanned PDFs have been through OCR. Adopt a **file-name convention** before the first import, because renaming later breaks the link to your master sheet and your survey.
notes.16: Build the attribute sheet in a spreadsheet and import it; typing one by one is where errors enter. **Match the survey's labels exactly** so the two datasets line up later. Keep facts known beforehand as attributes and keep your judgements as codes. Code focus-group speakers, or the group becomes one voice.
notes.17: Treat setup as insurance. The project file holds every transcript, so it needs encryption and daily backup. The first memo, written before any coding, is the **first draft of your methods section**. A new team member should be able to read it and understand what the project is for.
notes.18: Separate what you correct from what you leave alone. Fix labels, encoding, identifying details and transcription errors. Leave the respondent's grammar, dialect and hesitations and the interviewer's questions, because **cleaning speech into prose is editing the data**. Do all this in a word processor before import.
notes.19: Work down the checklist before the first code. Its length is the point: consent, storage, language, checking, translation, naming, pseudonyms, attributes and backup all sit upstream of analysis. The slide says a week for 36 interviews. **Protect that week**, because it is the one most often squeezed.
notes.21: Fill in all five fields of the codebook for every code: name, definition, use, do not use, example. The do-not-use line is what **keeps neighbouring codes apart**. Compare FEAR_FORMAL_FINANCE with MONEY_WORRY: a second coder can apply the first, while a bare word like 'fear' invites guessing.
notes.22: Learn this as seven steps, with the revision at step 4 as the one that matters. Code five transcripts closely, revise the codebook, then **recode those five** with the new version. It feels like repetition. The alternative is five transcripts coded under a codebook that no longer exists.
notes.23: Keep the tree shallow: two or three levels, and for 36 interviews about 40 to 80 codes after revision. Too many codes means nothing accumulates; too few means one code holds everything. A theme is a claim you build, so **never read the code tree as your findings**.
notes.24: Decide the segment size once and write it in the codebook. The working rule is the smallest unit that makes sense when retrieved, usually a sentence or two with its question. Use auto-coding by text only to find passages, and **budget eight to twelve transcript pages an hour** for coding by a person.
notes.25: Write a memo whenever you decide something, spot a pattern or feel surprised. Read the example memo twice: it holds a finding, a test, a hypothesis and a citation in one paragraph. Always **date your memos**, because their sequence is your audit trail and later feeds the methods section.
notes.26: Claim saturation only with evidence. The software can show new codes per transcript in the order coded, which gives you a curve. It cannot show what a different kind of respondent would have said. Name the subgroup the claim covers, and use the model sentence on the slide as your template.
notes.27: Read the columns left to right: definition, origin, then the counts. The origin column shows two inductive codes, SHIELD and STRATEGY, that **became the heart of the study** and were absent from the protocol. The counts help you orient, since a code in 22 of 36 files is widespread, but they are not findings.
notes.28: Tick through these twelve rows at the end of each coding stage. They apply equally in Taguette and in NVivo. Three deserve a pause: definitions for every code, a second person reviewing inductive codes, and treating text search as a way to find passages. A reviewer reads this list as **what 'systematic' means**.
notes.30: Start here if you have never coded. Taguette installs in minutes and covers text only: no audio, attributes or real memos. That limit is its virtue for a first project. Check the consent form before using the hosted version, since **your documents then sit on someone else's server**.
notes.31: Follow the six steps in order, and notice where each thing lives. Definitions go in the tag description, which is the only memo field, so keep analytic memos in a separate document. Build hierarchy with **punctuation in tag names**, such as SAVINGS.shield. Merging tags is how first-cycle codes become second-cycle ones.
notes.32: Team coding works only on a server, hosted or self-hosted. The local version is single-user. Agree the codebook in the tag descriptions first. For an agreement check, have coders use **prefixed tag sets** (A.SAVINGS, B.SAVINGS) on the same three documents, then compare the export in a spreadsheet.
notes.33: Learn the exports by what you want to do next. The codebook goes in the appendix, highlights by tag give you the evidence for a theme, and the .sqlite3 file is your backup. The **all-highlights CSV** is the most useful object, because joined with an attribute sheet it supports pivot tables for every count in section 07.
notes.34: Read the right-hand column as a list of exits. Each row names a need Taguette cannot meet and where to go. The slide gives you a practical trigger: when you build the **same pivot table by hand a third time**, move to a fuller tool. The codebook travels with you.
notes.35: If you teach or learn alone, borrow this sequence. Session 1 teaches what coding is. Session 2 puts two coders on one transcript so they disagree. Session 3 produces a theme memo. The slide's advice for session 2 is the one to follow: **do not resolve the disagreement for them**.
notes.36: Look at what twelve interviews and seven tags produced: a codebook, retrieval, a theme and an appendix. Then look at the limits. Two questions needed the spreadsheet: co-occurrence and attributes. That was **the cue to move up**. The study then grew to 36 interviews in two languages and went to QualCoder.
notes.38: QualCoder gives you most of what the paid tools offer, free and offline. It codes text, PDF, images, audio and video, and it compares coders. Note two practical details: audio and video need VLC, and any **LLM features stay off by default**. A student with an old laptop has everything needed.
notes.39: Use this as a floor plan. Files and cases hold the data, attributes hold the comparison variables, the coding screens do the daily work and the reports do the analysis. One instruction is easy to miss: **set your coder name before the first code**, because the comparison report depends on it.
notes.40: Memorise the loop: select, code, define. Create each new code with its memo at once, and keep annotations for 'come back to this' and memos for 'this is why'. For Indic text, set a font with full script coverage. Search is exact-string only, so **search roots and inflections separately**.
notes.41: Reach for audio coding when tone or speaker matters, especially in focus groups. Timestamps every minute make the transcript and audio scroll together. Code delivery on the audio and content on the transcript. If you skip the recording, **say so as a stated loss** in your methods.
notes.42: Use this table to find which report answers which question. The one you will open most is the **coding report filtered by attribute**, which turns 'what did non-members in Bihar say about the bank' into a document you can read. Treat text mining as orientation only and charts as aids to be used with care.
notes.43: REFI-QDA is why your first tool choice carries little risk. A .qdpx file moves codes, segments, memos, cases and attributes between tools. Tool-specific objects such as maps and some queries may drop out, so **check the import and keep the original**. Export one at every milestone as your archival copy.
notes.44: Follow the table as a timeline of one real-looking project. Notice three moments: the kappa rising for SHIELD after redefinition, the attribute retrieval that found 15 of 18 against 7 of 18, and the memos that became the first drafts. The slide itself says the **15 accounts are the finding**, and the number only points to them.
notes.46: Compare the three on their organising idea, because it shapes how you think. NVivo is built around queries, MAXQDA shows four windows at once, and ATLAS.ti treats quotations as objects. MAXQDA is gentlest to learn. Prices and features change yearly, so **verify with the vendor** before paying.
notes.47: Learn NVivo as a database with a query menu. Everything you build is a saved object you can rerun. Consistent speaker labels let it code speakers into cases in seconds, and the coding comparison query gives you kappa per code. Heed the cautions: **back up often**, and do not use English sentiment coding on Indian-language text.
notes.48: Picture four panes: documents, codes, the document being coded, and retrieved segments. The central move is activation: choose documents and codes and the retrieval updates. Document variables move to and from a spreadsheet, **bridging to your survey data**. This visibility is why many teachers prefer it.
notes.49: Think of ATLAS.ti as quotations first. A selected passage becomes an object with its own ID that you can link to other quotations. This suits discourse and narrative work, and suits counting codes less well. Its query tool has the **richest retrieval language** of the three, and its Web version suits distributed teams.
notes.50: Read the decision table from the top: if your institution licenses one tool, that is the answer, since support and a supervisor who can open your file matter most. The closing advice is practical: use the tool closest to hand for a first project, and **learn two over a career**.
notes.51: Before you pay, time your trial to an actual coding sprint and keep it away from an idle month. Check what your library already licenses. For cloud versions, **ask the vendor in writing** where data is stored, who can see it, whether it trains models and how to delete it. The answers decide whether the cloud is usable at all.
notes.52: Pick a transcription route by language and by who checks. Paid English-centred tools are weak for Hindi or Bangla. Machine routes for Indian languages are cheap but hallucinate in silence, so check every transcript. The slide's summary workflow is **machine draft, native-speaker pass, import**. Keep the audio as the truth.
notes.53: Migrate only at a milestone, never mid-coding. After the import, the test is simple: **code counts before and after must agree**. A mismatch of more than a handful means something was lost, and the original file is the record. Two coders on two tools can work through one exchange, but not by weekly swapping.
notes.55: Read before you count. A retrieval is every segment for one code, and reading it is your first hour of analysis. Always retrieve with context, meaning the question before and a sentence after. A retrieval of 300 segments is a signal that **the code needs splitting**.
notes.56: Read this matrix by files first and segments second. Ten of 12 Bihar members raised SHIELD, against one of seven non-members. That is a pattern worth a theme. Segment counts mostly show how much people talked. **Never report a cell as a population proportion**, because the sample was purposive.
notes.57: Use co-occurrence to decide what to read next. SHIELD and HUSBAND_DEMANDS overlapping in 19 segments tells you where the mechanism sits. The table depends on consistent segment size, since long segments overlap with everything. The slide's last line is the one to keep: it **finds where to look**, and you read what is there.
notes.58: Be wary of text tools on Indian languages. Stemming and stop lists are English, so a Hindi frequency table returns postpositions. Use text search to find passages for a known term and its variants, then read and code by hand. The slide is blunt about word clouds: **decoration that analyses nothing**.
notes.59: Chart each case against each theme in your own words, with a phrase quoted. Read a column to see the range of a theme and a row to see one woman's whole account. Sort rows by an attribute such as migrant husband to see if the column changes. **The charting is the analysis**, taking about three days for 36 cases.
notes.60: Before drawing a figure, ask what argument it carries. Most visuals in the table have a case where they help and a case where they mislead. A heat map invites readers to read shading as proportions. The slide's own verdict: the best figure is usually **a table of quotations by theme and case**.
notes.61: Walk the six links from pattern to check and test your own claim against them. The first three are fast with software. The last three, a claim with scope, evidence showing range, and a **search for disconfirming cases**, stay with you. A claim that came this way can be traced back through memo, query and segments.
notes.62: Tick these nine rows before you write findings. The slide singles out two: the third (no purposive cell as a population proportion) is the one a quantitative reader will test, and the seventh (every claim traceable) is the one a qualitative reviewer will. **Prepare for both readers.**
notes.64: Teams exist for capacity, language coverage and a second reading. Make four arrangements before anyone codes: one owned and versioned codebook, weekly meetings, coder names set in the software and an agreed merge protocol. The interviewer codes best and worst for the same reason, so **pair them with a second reader**.
notes.65: Measure agreement only when the method expects consistent application, as in content, framework and template analysis. Report kappa **per code**, never as one average for forty codes. Skip it for reflexive thematic analysis, where codes are the researcher's interpretation. A low kappa tells you the definition needs work.
notes.66: Follow what the table did. SHIELD was redefined and rose from 0.58 to 0.79. DECISION_STRATEGY was split into three codes, and one of those turned out analytically useful. Percentage agreement runs high because most text is uncoded, and kappa corrects for that. **Measure, act, then measure again.**
notes.67: Choose among three merging arrangements before coding starts. The usual desktop route is to divide the files and merge copies. Its main risk is codebook drift, which you manage by letting **only the codebook owner create codes**. Test the merge on two small copies first, and keep every coder's copy until it is verified.
notes.68: When two coders work in two languages, give them one bilingual codebook with source-language anchors. Agreement on the English translations tests whether the codebook travels, and says nothing about whether the coders read the languages alike. A code that means something different in Bangla is **a finding in its own right**.
notes.69: Treat versioning as a table of habits. Back up daily to a second place, save a dated version at each milestone, export the codebook at each revision, and keep a dated project log. The slide's claim is worth testing on yourself: with these habits an examiner **can audit you in an afternoon**.
notes.70: Use this list at the start of the coding period. The slide notes that the third row, testing the merge before it matters, fails most often, since teams merge for the first time on deadline day. **Run a trial merge in week two** and tick the rest as they happen.
notes.72: Integration means making the survey and the interviews answer each other. The survey gives the size of an effect and the interviews give the how and for whom. Pick your point: **connecting, building or merging**. The software's biggest contribution is attributes, so interviewees who are also survey respondents carry their survey values.
notes.73: Read the third column first. A joint display is one table with survey result, qualitative finding and an integrated reading beside each other. The third row is the useful kind, because **the strands disagree and the disagreement explains the survey's null**. That integrated paragraph is what a policy reader remembers.
notes.74: Open-ended survey answers are qualitative data at scale. Import them as cases with attributes, code with a short codebook, and export a 0/1 matrix back to the survey file. Counting is legitimate here because the denominator is the survey sample. Check agreement on **a ten per cent sample** as in section 08.
notes.75: Use survey records to select interviewees on purpose: maximum variation on the outcome, extreme cases, or strata by a moderator. Then the interviews explain the numbers with the numbers attached. The slide highlights **deviant cases**, such as a member who declined, as often the most informative interviews in the study.
notes.76: Apply one rule to every count: what is the denominator? A defined sample answering a defined question makes a count a statistic. A purposive set of conversations makes it a pointer, and the sentence must say so. Go through the six rows and say which is **proportion, description or pointer**.
notes.77: Use this grid to see how far each tool takes you on its own. MAXQDA builds joint displays and runs statistics inside the project. The others get there through an export and a table in Word or a pivot table, which the slide puts at **a morning's work**. Choose MAXQDA when integration is the centre of the study.
notes.78: Tick these nine rows when a survey exists. They move from stating the integration point to weaving the strands in the report instead of stacking separate chapters. Two to watch: label every count by its denominator, and report disagreement between strands. **Suppressing a mismatch** throws away the most useful finding.
notes.80: Match each of Lincoln and Guba's four criteria to what your project file can show. Credibility needs the retrievals and negative cases, transferability needs attributes and a sampling memo, dependability needs the log and codebook versions, and confirmability needs reflexive memos. **Keep the file as sections 03 and 08 describe.**
notes.81: Treat the left list as a folder structure you build as you go. Then rehearse the examiner's questions: how you reached theme three, how you handled the Bangla interviews, who coded what. Each has a document behind it. The slide's point is that none of this is extra work, because **it is the project**.
notes.82: Write the first reflexive memo before the first interview, listing expectations, worries and what would surprise you. Add one when you are surprised and one when a theme feels settled. In the report, name constraints such as an implementer-commissioned study and add a sentence **wherever position could shape a finding**.
notes.83: Choose the checks you can afford and describe them accurately. Member checking works better on synthesised findings than on transcripts. Negative case analysis uses the cases that contradict you, which mark the boundary of your theme. Peer debriefing means a blind second coding. **None is a guarantee**, and each is a paragraph in the methods.
notes.84: Give the reader enough to judge whether your finding applies in Odisha or Sindh. Describe the sample by the attributes that mattered, such as migration and group rules, plus the programme as delivered and the interviews themselves. The example shows that **three attributes** produced the transferability argument.
notes.85: Treat COREQ and SRQR as an index of what the project file already holds. COREQ's three domains map onto reflexive memos, sampling and translation memos, and the codebook and agreement table. Fill the checklist against your draft. **Every item you cannot answer is a gap** to close before submission.
notes.86: Select quotations to show range, including edges, and introduce each one before it appears. Check per-participant consent for quotation and paraphrase where it was withheld. In small places, generalise attributes: 'a group office-bearer' protects what a village-level label would expose. Keep a **quotation log** of every source.
notes.87: Read this paragraph as an answer key: each number points to a file, memo or report in the project. That is what 'systematic' means. Try writing yours from your own project and see which clauses you cannot support. The slide warns that many reports offer **the paragraph without the evidence behind it**.
notes.88: Sort every project object into deposit, deposit with conditions, or never. The codebook always goes in. The coded project without transcripts usually can, after you check memos for identifying detail. The quotation log stays with the consent forms. This table is also **your data availability statement** for funders.
notes.90: Start with the last column. Every AI feature in these tools sends transcript text to an external model, which decides whether it is usable under your consent and policy. Taguette has none, and QualCoder's is off by default. **Opt-in is the common rule**, so no feature turns itself on.
notes.91: Match each risk to its practice. Data leaving the machine needs consent that names external processing. Hallucinated summaries mean every output is checked against the retrieval. Homogenisation and weak Indian-language performance mean testing with a bilingual reader. The defensible example is **a reading aid, disclosed and checked**.
notes.92: Validate AI the way you would a second coder: same codebook, same eight files, kappa per code. In the table the model reaches 0.77 on SAVINGS_PURPOSE but only 0.41 on SAVINGS_SHIELD. Use it where it agrees and **keep interpretive codes human**. Budget real review time, and revalidate when the model or the codebook changes.
notes.93: Write your disclosure before you start the analysis. Make three statements: the software and version, how transcripts were produced and checked, and any AI assistance with data seen, consent basis and limit. If it **cannot be written accurately, the use should not happen**. Where no AI was used, say so in one sentence.
notes.94: Use this table to match your situation to a tool, then read the last row. It makes the general point: invest in the codebook, the memos and the archive, because the software is **only where they live this year**. Any REFI-QDA tool keeps your work portable when staff or licences change.
notes.95: Use the eight weeks as a planning template and notice the proportions. Week 1 is preparation, week 8 is writing, and the middle weeks are coding, agreement and matrices. The slide says the checking week was the best-spent. The archive at the bottom is **enough to follow every step and identifies no one**.
notes.96: Scan the twelve errors for the ones you are about to make. Each has a section and a one-line fix. Several share a root: skipping a definition, a check or a consent question. Your cheapest insurance is an early habit, such as **testing the merge in week two** instead of on deadline day.
notes.97: Run this fifteen-line list before you submit. It splits into data and process, then analysis and reporting. The slide names two items most often missing from South Asian reports: the **translation workflow and the AI disclosure**. Do those two first, then work through the rest.
notes.98: Pick the readings that match your next step. Saldaña supports coding, Gale et al. the framework method, Braun and Clarke thematic analysis, O'Connor and Joffe the agreement debate, and Tong and O'Brien the reporting. The CAQDAS Networking Project offers **comparative reviews of every package**. The tool manuals are free.
notes.99: Use this as a final review. Cover the slide and try to restate each statement from memory. The closing line gives the test your project should pass: an examiner can walk from any theme back to the recording **in ten minutes**. Build for that reader from the first memo.
